prompt: A fly has six legs and a spider has eight legs. A group of three flies and two spiders has the same number of legs in total as a group of seven chickens and some dogs. How many dogs are in the second group?

solutions.title: Count legs
solutions.body:
The first group has $3\times6+2\times8=34$ legs. Seven chickens have 14 legs, so the dogs have $34-14=20$ legs, which is $20\div4=5$ dogs.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: Sritha has four copies of a straight strip of three squares in a row (a $1\times3$ rectangle). Which of the following could she not make from her four copies?

solutions.title: Look at the ends
solutions.body:
In shape E, the squares at the ends of the two prongs on the left and the two squares at the end of the spike on the right can only be covered by horizontal strips. That forces strips that leave three squares not connected in a row, which cannot be covered by the fourth strip. The other four shapes can each be tiled by four strips.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: The diagram shows a lake containing 10 islands linked with 12 bridges. What is the smallest number of bridges that would need to be closed to prevent anyone walking from island P to island Q?

solutions.title: Two disjoint routes
solutions.body:
There is an upper route and a lower route from P to Q that share no bridge, so closing one bridge is never enough. Closing one bridge on each route (for example one of the two bridges leaving P at the bottom, and one of the final bridges into Q on the upper route) cuts both. So the minimum is 2.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: Amy and Beth are solving Maths puzzles. Beth can solve three puzzles in the time Amy can solve two. Between them they solved 30 puzzles. How many more puzzles than Amy did Beth solve?

solutions.title: Blocks of time
solutions.body: In one block, Beth solves 3 and Amy 2: 5 in total. $30\div5=6$ blocks, and in each Beth solves 1 more, so 6 more.

solutions.title: Ratio
solutions.body:
They solve in the ratio $3:2$, so Beth solves $18$ and Amy $12$. The difference is 6.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: The mean of a set of five different positive integers is 4. What is the largest integer that could be in the set?

solutions.title: Make the others small
solutions.body:
The total is 20. The four smallest other numbers are at least $1+2+3+4=10$, so the largest is at most $20-10=10$, achieved by $1,2,3,4,10$.

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: A furniture store is selling sofas, love seats and chairs made from two types of identical modular pieces plus a back piece, as shown viewed from above. Including the armrests, the width of the sofa is 220 cm and the width of the love seat is 160 cm. What is the width, in cm, of the chair?

solutions.title: Each extra seat
solutions.body:
The sofa has one more seat than the love seat, so a seat is $220-160=60$ cm wide. The chair has one fewer seat than the love seat: $160-60=100$ cm.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: The five keys shown fit the five padlocks. The numbers on the keys are coded by letters on the padlocks. The padlocks are DAD, BHD, AHD, ABD, HAB and the keys are 184, 812, 124, 414 and one more with a question mark. Which number is written on the remaining key?

solutions.title: Decode
solutions.body:
Only DAD has equal first and third letters, matching 414: $D=4$, $A=1$. AHD and ABD match 124 and 184 (so $B,H$ are 2 and 8 in some order). The key 812 must be HAB, so $H=8$, $B=2$. The missing key fits BHD: $2,8,4$, i.e. 284.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: Pierre writes all the numbers from 1 to 20 in a row and obtains the 31-digit number 1234567891011121314151617181920. He then deletes 24 of the 31 digits so that the remaining number is as large as possible. Which number does he get?

solutions.title: Greedy choice
solutions.body:
He keeps 7 digits. Delete the first eight digits to start with 9. A second 9 appears only three digits from the end, too late to leave 6 more digits, and an 8 after the first 9 is also too late. A 7 (from 17) leaves six digits 181920 available, then 8, 1, 9, 2, 0 follow: 9781920.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: When Katarina added the two numbers in each row and each column of the grid $\begin{array}{|c|c|}\hline a&b\\\hline c&d\\\hline\end{array}$, she obtained the results shown: row sums 2 (top) and 3 (bottom), column sums 1 (left) and 4 (right). Which of the statements below is true?

solutions.title: Compare the sums
solutions.body:
$a+b=2$ and $a+c=1$ give $b=c+1$, so $b>c$ (B and D false). $a+c=1$ and $c+d=3$ give $d=a+2$, so $a<d$.

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: Kush spent five days walking in the mountains. He started on Monday and his last day was Friday. Each day he walked 2 km more than he had done the day before. The total distance he walked was 70 km. What distance did Kush walk on Thursday?

solutions.title: Middle day
solutions.body:
The five distances form an arithmetic sequence, so the mean is the middle (Wednesday) value: $70\div5=14$. Thursday is $14+2=16$ km.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: On Iyla's island there are some lions, some tigers and some jaguars. Two-thirds of the animals are not lions; three-quarters of the animals are not tigers; 84 of the animals are not jaguars. How many animals are on Iyla's island?

solutions.title: Equation
solutions.body:
With $y$ animals, lions are $\frac13y$ and tigers $\frac14y$. Animals that are not jaguars are lions or tigers: $\frac7{12}y=84$, so $y=144$.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: How many positive integers between 10 and 2026 have all their digits the same and are divisible by 3?

solutions.title: Count by length
solutions.body:
Two digits: 33, 66, 99. Three digits: all nine ($111,\dots,999$) are divisible by 3 (digit sum $3d$). Four digits below 2026: only 1111, not divisible by 3. Total $3+9=12$.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: Beads numbered 1 to $n$, where $n>1$, are threaded onto a bracelet. What is the smallest value of $n$ for which this can be done in such a way that no two consecutive numbers are next to each other?

solutions.title: Test small n
solutions.body:
With 3 beads, bead 2 is next to both 1 and 3. With 4 beads, bead 2 has two neighbours among the three others, so at least one of 1 and 3 is next to it. With 5 beads, arrange 1, 4, 2, 5, 3 round the bracelet: neighbouring pairs (1,4), (4,2), (2,5), (5,3), (3,1) have no consecutive numbers. So $n=5$.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: Five children each writes down a different positive integer. One writes down a square, one writes down a cube, one writes down a prime, one writes down an odd integer and one writes down an even integer. What is the smallest possible total of the five integers?

solutions.title: Lower bound and example
solutions.body:
Five different positive integers sum to at least $1+2+3+4+5=15$. This is achievable: 1 is a cube, 4 a square, 2 is even (and prime is 3), 5 is odd. So 15.

**Answer: (A)**

prompt: In an orchard, 80% of the trees were apple trees and the rest were pear trees. Last summer, the apple weevil killed some of the apple trees but no pear trees. Now 50% of the trees are apple trees. What percentage of the apple trees were killed by the apple weevil?

solutions.title: Use 100 trees
solutions.body:
Start with 80 apple and 20 pear trees. Pear trees are unchanged and are now 50% of the total, so 20 apple trees remain. $60$ died: $\frac{60}{80}=75\%$.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: The integers 1 to 20 are written on a board. Patricia erases three of the integers and replaces them with their sum. She repeats this process until only two integers remain. What is the sum of these two remaining integers?

solutions.title: Invariant
solutions.body:
Replacing three numbers by their sum keeps the total of all numbers on the board. The total starts at $1+2+\dots+20=210$, so the two remaining integers sum to 210.

**Answer: (E)**

prompt: Four players each scored goals in a handball match. Each of them scored a different number of goals. Of the four, Will scored the fewest goals. The other three scored twenty goals in total. What is the largest number of goals Will could have scored?

solutions.title: Push the minimum up
solutions.body:
The other three scored at least $w+1$ each, all different. If Will scored 5, the others are at least $6+7+8=21>20$. If Will scored 4, the others could be $5,7,8$ (sum 20). So 4.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: Rafael uses three squares to create a shape. The first has side-length 3 cm. The second has side-length 5 cm and one of its vertices is placed in the centre of the first square. The third square has side-length 7 cm and one of its vertices is placed in the centre of the second square, as shown in the diagram. The top edges of all three squares are parallel. What is the total shaded area in $\text{cm}^2$?

solutions.title: Inclusion-exclusion
solutions.body:
The overlaps are squares with sides $1.5$ cm (half of 3) and $2.5$ cm (half of 5). Area $=9+25+49-2.25-6.25=74.5$.

**Answer: (B)**

prompt: Nell wants to write the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 in the five cells in the diagram (a row of three cells with two further cells below the first) so that any number directly below another number is greater than that number and any number directly to the right of another number is greater than that number. In how many ways can she do this?

solutions.title: Start at the corner
solutions.body:
The top-left cell is left of two cells and above two, so it holds 1. The number 2 goes in the cell to its right or the cell below it. Say 2 is to the right: the third cell of the top row can be 3, 4 or 5, and the remaining two numbers go in the column in increasing order: 3 ways. By symmetry another 3 ways. Total 6.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: Ali said Dele ate the cake. Dele said Billi ate the cake. Billi said Callie ate the cake. Callie said she didn't eat the cake and Eddie said that he did. I know Ali didn't eat the cake, that one of the others did and that only one of them is telling the truth. Who ate the cake?

solutions.title: Test Callie
solutions.body:
If Callie told the truth, everyone else lies, so none of Dele, Billi, Eddie and Ali ate the cake and nobody ate it. Contradiction, so Callie lied: she ate the cake. (Then only Billi told the truth.)

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: Eight kangaroos stood in a line, as shown. At some point, two kangaroos standing next to each other and facing each other exchanged places. This was repeated until no further exchanges were possible. How many exchanges were made?

solutions.title: Count crossings
solutions.body:
Three kangaroos face left. The first left-facing kangaroo has 3 right-facing kangaroos on its left, so it makes 3 exchanges. The other two left-facing kangaroos each have 5 right-facing kangaroos on their left and make 5 exchanges. Total $3+5+5=13$.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: A bag contains only red marbles and green marbles. For every five marbles that are chosen, at least one will be red. For every six marbles that are chosen, at least one will be green. What is the largest number of marbles the bag can contain?

solutions.title: Bound each colour
solutions.body:
There cannot be five green marbles (we could choose five with no red), so at most 4 green. Similarly at most 5 red. So at most 9, and 4 green with 5 red works.

**Answer: (C)**

prompt: Freda likes even numbers, Greta likes numbers divisible by 3 and Hattie likes numbers divisible by 5. A basket contains eight balls, each with a number written on. The three girls went in turn to the basket and took all the balls with a number on that they like. Freda collected balls with numbers 32 and 52 on, Greta collected balls with numbers 24, 33 and 45 on and Hattie collected balls with numbers 20, 25 and 35 on. In what order did the girls go to the basket?

solutions.title: Look at shared balls
solutions.body:
Greta took 24 (even) and 45 (multiple of 5), so she went before Freda and Hattie. Hattie took 20 (even), so she went before Freda. Order: Greta, Hattie, Freda.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: Jacques wants to write a positive integer in each box in the diagram (a pyramid of 1, 2, 3 and 4 boxes in rows) so that each integer above the bottom row is the sum of the two integers immediately below it. What is the largest number of odd integers that Jacques can write?

solutions.title: Parity
solutions.body:
If the bottom row is all odd, every box above is even: only 4 odd. If the second row from the bottom is all odd, the top two rows are all even: only 5 odd. To beat these, each of the bottom two rows must contain an even number, and the top two rows must also contain an even number (two odd numbers sum to an even number, and odd plus even gives odd, so if the top row and second row were all odd it would fail). That makes at least 3 even numbers out of 10, so at most 7 odd. Example: bottom row $1,2,1,1$; next row $3,3,2$; next $6,5$; top $11$. The odd numbers are $1,1,1,3,3,5,11$: seven.

**Answer: (D)**

prompt: Julia has four different coloured pencils and wants to use some or all of them to colour the map of four regions shown in the diagram. She wants to ensure that two regions that share a common border are shaded in different colours. In how many different ways can she colour the map?

solutions.title: Colour in order
solutions.body:
Label the regions $P,Q,R,S$ where $P$ borders all three others, $R$ borders $P$ and $Q$ and $S$, and $S$ borders $P$ and $R$ but not $Q$. $P$: 4 choices, $Q$: 3, $R$: 2 (different from $P,Q$), $S$: 2 (different from $P,R$). Total $4\times3\times2\times2=48$.

**Answer: (E)**
